title: What If You Never Needed Sleep Again?
script: What if you never needed sleep again? Not less sleep. Not ever. Night one, it's three in the morning and you've finished your homework, learned three songs on guitar, and reorganized the fridge. In 1964, a teenager set a famous record by staying awake about eleven days, and by the end he could barely think straight. But your body skips the crash. Day twelve, you're still wide awake and feeling great. Then something weird starts happening. Day fifteen, one of your guitar songs is just gone. Day twenty, your little brother Sam asks if you liked his first goal. You were there. You can't remember it. Here's why. While you sleep, your brain replays the day and saves it, like hitting save in a game. You never sleep, so you never hit save. Then, on night forty, you smell smoke. Everyone in your building is asleep, and sleeping people often don't wake up to the smell of smoke. So you run floor to floor, banging on every door, until forty people are standing outside in their pajamas, safe. Next morning, a doctor hands you one pill. Take it tonight, and you'll sleep and remember again, forever. Ten seconds. Nine. Eight. Sam is asleep down the hall, and you've already lost his first goal. Seven. Six. Your grandma lives on the top floor, and she sleeps right through her smoke alarm. Five. Four. Your brother's memories, or your grandma's nights. Would you ever sleep again?

hud.label: REAL SCIENCE
hud.text: 1964 record: about 11 days awake. By the end, a foggy brain.

hud.label: REAL SCIENCE
hud.text: Sleep helps your brain save the day's memories.

hud.label: REAL SCIENCE
hud.text: The smell of smoke often doesn't wake sleeping people.

hud.label: THE COST
hud.text: Sleep again. Nobody awake at 3 AM.
